routeSelection.basis: The generic target has two equally formal specialisations, Society and Policy and Ecology and Conservation. Neither is clearly broader or less specialised, so the first current handbook specialisation is selected before considering UCR fit.

alternatives.label: Ecology, nature and environmental governance
alternatives.labelReason: Strong ecological core combined with actual environmental law, economic foundations, institutions, justice and human-environment research.
alternatives.concept: Combine biodiversity, ecological processes and environmental systems with law, economics, institutions and social-environmental research to examine conservation decisions. Water, climate and land-use pressures connect environmental evidence with public action. Dedicated tree and forest-management training remains a difference.
progression: Current workbook offerings and earlier formal prerequisites verified for all24courses. PPD is in Year1; 6advanced courses. Core ecology precedes advanced marine/farming study where selected; mathematical, legal, laboratory and economic-method prerequisites are earlier. Open-curriculum advisory progression does not add formal gates.

alternatives.label: Ecology, biodiversity and environmental investigation
alternatives.labelReason: Replaces weak human-biomedical selections with concrete soil, geospatial, environmental chemistry and resource-impact investigation while retaining biodiversity and ecosystem processes.
alternatives.concept: Study species, evolutionary relationships and ecosystem functioning alongside soils, water, climate, geospatial observation and environmental measurement. Laboratory and field methods, ecological models and resource-impact assessment support conservation questions across terrestrial, delta and marine environments; this does not reproduce specialist forestry.
alternatives.distinctness: Eight courses unique against the closest programme prioritise ecological/soil/spatial/physical investigation and resource-impact methods over its sustained legal/social/political strand.
progression: Current workbook offerings and earlier formal prerequisites verified for all24courses. PPD is in Year1; 7advanced courses. Core ecology precedes advanced marine/farming study where selected; mathematical, legal, laboratory and economic-method prerequisites are earlier. Open-curriculum advisory progression does not add formal gates.

alternatives.label: Nature policy, institutions and environmental evidence
alternatives.labelReason: Prioritises environmental institutions, externalities, empirical policy evidence and communication with substantive environmental process and resource content.
alternatives.concept: Examine environmental governance through law, public economics, political institutions, justice and communication. Empirical research, data and causal analysis inform policy evaluation, while water, soils, resource pressures and remediation supply an environmental foundation. The priority is social-environmental decisions rather than a full ecology or forestry sequence.
alternatives.distinctness: Ten courses unique against the closest and eleven against ecology prioritise governance, public economics, causal evidence, law and institutional processes over species/population/ecological study. Curricular differences implement these priorities, not arbitrary swaps.
progression: Current workbook offerings and earlier formal prerequisites verified for all24courses. PPD is in Year1; 7advanced courses. Core ecology precedes advanced marine/farming study where selected; mathematical, legal, laboratory and economic-method prerequisites are earlier. Open-curriculum advisory progression does not add formal gates.

core: Biodiversity, ecological processes, forest and nature management
People, institutions, policy and natural-resource governance
Water, soils, landscapes, climate and spatial evidence
Field, quantitative and social-environmental research methods
questions: How can ecological and social evidence guide conservation?
How can resource conflicts and ecosystem pressures be governed?

candidates.label: Forest and Landscape dual-degree context
candidates.reason: The separately confirmed Alnarp dual-degree direction is accounted for but not attempted after three defensible programmes. Its location-dependent curriculum is not mixed into the ordinary Wageningen comparator.

trace: Consumer/producer choices, scarcity, incentives and strategic interaction provide economic foundations for natural-resource decisions; not a complete environmental-economics course.

Public goods, externalities, collective choice and efficiency/equity evaluation directly support environmental-policy instruments and distributional trade-offs, though applications extend beyond nature.
Description-supported OLS/GLS/instrumental variables, causal and predictive inference, Monte Carlo simulation and an empirical paper strengthen quantitative evaluation of policy evidence.

Operationalisation, sampling, surveys, experimental/nonexperimental research, R analysis and a substantial empirical project support human-environment research design; no ecological fieldwork guaranteed.
R cleaning, joining, visualisation and geospatial/tabular data projects support environmental and governance evidence handling.
Calculus, differential equations and a dynamic-model project provide quantitative tools for changing environmental systems.
Probability, sampling, estimation, tests, uncertainty and Monte Carlo methods support interpretation of ecological/environmental data.
Water quantity/quality, salinisation, freshwater scarcity, nature-based responses and place-based adaptation planning integrate hydrological and social consequences for delta landscapes.
Plant/mycelium soil remediation, metal-contaminant measurement, experimental protocols and recovery-yield analysis provide concrete ecological restoration and resource-circularity complements.

Institutions, power, participation, stakeholder matrices and policy evaluation/advice directly develop environmental governance and collective sustainability decisions, without promising a forest-specific project.
Tree-of-life diversity, organism identification, microscopy and biodiversity indices directly support observation and monitoring of species and habitats.
Habitat fragmentation, extinction, species management and conservation planning directly implement biodiversity protection; a local threatened-species project evaluates protection measures.
Population genetics, adaptation, speciation, phylogeny and biogeography explain variation and evolutionary relationships needed to understand species conservation.
Population/community/ecosystem dynamics, energy and matter cycles and ecological modelling in R directly support ecosystem functioning and conservation evidence.
Marine habitats, productivity, microbial ecology and fisheries/acidification impacts extend ecosystem conservation to marine and estuarine systems; not forest ecology or a field-methods course.
Agricultural biodiversity impacts and comparative appraisal of farming innovations address land-use pressures on ecosystems; not silviculture or forest-resource inventory.
Rock/mineral identification, geological mapping, stratigraphy and Ardennes field investigation develop the geological landscape context and field observation used in environmental analysis.
Description-supported drought, climate-driven hazards, mining disasters and toxic algal blooms develop specific environmental-risk analysis and adaptation; not forest-management planning.
ArcGIS Pro, georeferencing, spatial databases, remote sensing and environmental case analysis directly implement spatial environmental evidence; no generic Earth-system proxy substitute for GIS.
Soil formation/quality, soil biology, coring, chemical testing and aquifer geophysics provide concrete soil-water field and laboratory methods relevant to habitat conditions.
Description-supported biosphere-water-rock-atmosphere interactions, system models, proxies/isotope tracers and greenhouse-gas fieldwork provide environmental-process tools; not GIS training.
Redox, adsorption, weathering and biological-chemical soil/water interactions, geochemical modelling and remediation laboratories support environmental quality and ecosystem substrate analysis.

Description-supported geoscience investigation of carbon storage, waste storage and geothermal resource use develops assessment of land/resource pressures and literature-based technical reporting; not ecological forest inventory.
Nutrient cycles, acidification, planetary boundaries, environmental models and chemical/physical measurement establish how environmental pressures affect ecosystems; no forestry specialism inferred.
Chemical/material analysis and evidence-based evaluation of sustainability claims support environmental investigation and scrutiny of proposed resource-use solutions.

Climate feedbacks, tipping points, acidification, sea-level change and ecosystem/agricultural impacts directly inform conservation pressures and adaptation; stakeholder communication adds a specific social response.

Life-cycle assessment projects evaluate environmental impacts from resource extraction through reuse and disposal, providing methods to assess consumption/resource pressures rather than forest-specific production management.
Legal interpretation, public/private law, property and justice provide foundations for resource rights and later environmental-law reasoning; not human geography.
International legal instruments, environmental protection, compliance and treaty politics directly support cross-border environmental governance; not full Dutch administrative/environmental law.
Political institutions, participation, interest groups and empirical comparison explain the institutional setting of nature-policy decisions; not specialised public administration.
International institutions, colonial relations, climate politics and negotiation simulations complement cross-border natural-resource governance; not management of conservation organisations.
EU institutions, agenda setting, decision-making and legislative-process research support multilevel environmental policymaking; not strategic protected-area management.

Description-supported social-movement theory, Environmental Justice Atlas cases and feminist/anticolonial/degrowth perspectives directly examine environmental participation, resource conflicts and unequal impacts.
Description-supported climate arguments, contested public texts/media and a public-debate project develop environmental communication and critique; not a guaranteed focus-group methods course.

selection.assessment: The broad closest programme is followed by a substantively different ecological/environmental investigation programme and then a policy/institutions/evidence programme. Actual curricular priorities produce8/10/11unique-course pairwise differences. All three pass feasibility after current-offering repairs; stop at three. Dual-degree evidence is accounted for but no fourth candidate is attempted.

notes.text: The UCR programmes combine conservation, environmental systems and governance in different ways. They do not reproduce the full tree and forest-management sequence, specialist protected-area planning, compulsory joint ecological/social field courses or required 12-credit thesis. Optional UCR research is additional to each 180-credit schedule.

audience.programmeDescription: Forest and Nature Conservation combines ecology and biodiversity with the social relationships, policy and management of forests, natural areas and landscapes.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Three UCR programmes develop related interests through different priorities: ecological and social conservation questions, environmental investigation, or policy and institutions. Specialist forestry, structured conservation fieldwork and the required Wageningen thesis remain important differences.
